facts.title: The Only Liquid Metal
facts.text: Mercury is the only metallic element that is liquid at ordinary room temperature, staying fluid from its freezing point of -38.83 degrees Celsius all the way up to 356.73 degrees Celsius. This happens because mercury's outer electrons are held so tightly by relativistic effects that the atoms barely share them, leaving the metallic bonds unusually weak. Only the nonmetal bromine joins it as a liquid element under normal conditions.

facts.title: Named for a Planet and a God
facts.text: Mercury's chemical symbol Hg comes from the Latin word hydrargyrum, meaning water-silver, a translation of the Greek term for the shiny, flowing metal. Its English name honors the Roman messenger god Mercury, famed for his speed, just as the planet Mercury was named for racing quickly around the Sun. The element has been known since at least 1500 BCE and was found in Egyptian tombs.

facts.title: Relativity You Can Pour
facts.text: The reason mercury is a liquid is a striking everyday example of Einstein's relativity. Electrons in mercury's inner shells move at a large fraction of the speed of light, gaining effective mass and pulling the 6s electrons close to the nucleus. These contracted electrons resist bonding with neighboring atoms, so mercury cannot lock into a solid lattice at room temperature the way other metals do.

facts.title: It Climbed Into Thermometers
facts.text: Because mercury expands very evenly as it warms and does not stick to glass, Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit used it to build the first reliable mercury thermometer in 1714. The same uniform expansion made mercury the heart of barometers, blood-pressure cuffs, and thermostats for centuries. Many of these instruments are now being phased out worldwide to reduce toxic mercury pollution.

facts.title: A Poison That Maddened Hatters
facts.text: Mercury is a potent neurotoxin, and chronic exposure to mercury compounds in 19th-century felt-hat making caused tremors, slurred speech, and personality changes, the origin of the phrase mad as a hatter. The element accumulates in the brain and kidneys and can cross the placenta. In 1956, an industrial dump of methylmercury into Japan's Minamata Bay poisoned thousands and gave its name to Minamata disease.

facts.title: Cinnabar, Its Fiery Ore
facts.text: Mercury rarely appears as a free metal in nature; most of it is locked in a brilliant red ore called cinnabar, which is mercury sulfide. Roasting cinnabar in air releases mercury vapor that is then condensed back into liquid metal. Ground cinnabar was prized as the pigment vermilion and colored everything from ancient Roman frescoes to Chinese lacquerware.

facts.title: Gold's Liquid Magnet
facts.text: Mercury readily dissolves many metals, including gold and silver, forming soft alloys called amalgams. Gold miners have long exploited this by mixing mercury with crushed ore to capture tiny gold flecks, then boiling the mercury away. Dentists used silver-mercury amalgam fillings for over 150 years because the paste is soft enough to shape yet hardens into a durable, long-lasting solid.

facts.title: Glowing in Every Streetlight
facts.text: When an electric current passes through mercury vapor, it emits ultraviolet and blue-green light, the principle behind fluorescent tubes and the old bluish mercury-vapor street lamps. In fluorescent bulbs the UV strikes a phosphor coating that re-emits visible light, making them far more efficient than incandescent bulbs. This is why even modern compact fluorescent lamps contain a few milligrams of mercury.

facts.title: Heavier Than Iron Cannonballs
facts.text: Mercury is astonishingly dense at about 13.5 grams per cubic centimeter, roughly 13.5 times denser than water and heavier than lead by volume's feel. An iron cannonball or a lump of lead will actually float on a pool of liquid mercury rather than sink. This great density is what let a short column of mercury in a barometer balance the entire weight of the atmosphere.

facts.title: A Frozen World Shares Its Name
facts.text: The planet Mercury, the solar system's smallest and innermost planet, was named for the same swift god, but it is not made of the metal. Curiously, NASA's MESSENGER spacecraft confirmed in 2012 that the planet hides large deposits of frozen water ice in permanently shadowed craters near its poles, despite daytime temperatures exceeding 400 degrees Celsius. The metal mercury, meanwhile, is forged in stars and scattered by supernova explosions.
